lengthsNote: Metres, typical adult. ankleHeight: floor→ankle joint. footFront / heel: ball of the foot in front of / heel behind the ankle. midfoot: balance point in front of the ankle. trunk: hip→shoulder joint. hipHalfWidth / shoulderHalfWidth: midline→hip / shoulder joint. chestDepth: height of the bar on the chest above the shoulder joints, lying on a bench.
trunkPartsNote: For the holding muscles (lower and upper back): head and trunk split as in de Leva's table (fraction of body mass; together = headTrunk). Placed along the hip → shoulder line: head 0.13 m above the shoulders, upper trunk halfway between mid-back and shoulders, middle trunk 70% of the way from L5/S1 to mid-back (positions estimated). l5s1: the lumbosacral joint, metres above the hip joints along the trunk (estimate, TODO: source).

lower-back.note: A typical man's isometric lower-back (L5/S1) extension strength in lifting postures: about 270 N·m, where Tan et al. (295 N·m with the trunk bent 35°), Gallagher (265–270 N·m at 22.5–45°) and Mawston et al. (212–227 N·m in a maximal lift) roughly agree. Upright it is less (Tan et al. 150, Graves et al. 238 N·m). Dolan et al. measured 430 N·m pulling from the floor with the spine flexed (passive tissues add up to 120 N·m fully flexed), and national-level powerlifters reach up to about 990 N·m in deadlifts (Cholewicki et al.), so trained lifters are far stronger: use the strength slider. Taken as the same at every trunk angle (the spine is held neutral).
lower-back.source: Tan JC, Parnianpour M, Nordin M, Hofer H, Willems B (1993). Isometric maximal and submaximal trunk extension at different flexed positions in standing. Spine 18(16):2480–2490. doi:10.1097/00007632-199312000-00018 (Fig. 6: 31 men, standing, about L5/S1: about 150, 225 and 295 N·m upright, 15° and 35° bent, read off the figure); Gallagher S (1997). Trunk extension strength and muscle activity in standing and kneeling postures. Spine 22(16):1864–1872. doi:10.1097/00007632-199708150-00011 (Fig. 2: 21 men, standing, isometric medians about 200, 195 and 142 ft·lb, i.e. 270, 265 and 193 N·m, at 22.5°, 45° and 67.5° of trunk flexion, read off the figure); Mawston G, Holder L, O'Sullivan P, Boocock M (2021). Flexed lumbar spine postures are associated with greater strength and efficiency than lordotic postures during a maximal lift in pain-free individuals. Gait Posture 86:245–250. doi:10.1016/j.gaitpost.2021.02.029 (Table 2: 13 men, maximal lift: 212, 217 and 227 N·m with the back arched, mid-range and rounded); range: Dolan P, Mannion AF, Adams MA (1994). Passive tissues help the back muscles to generate extensor moments during lifting. J Biomech 27(8):1077–1085. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(94)90224-0 (Table 1: 23 men, isometric pull from the floor with the lumbar spine 70% flexed: 430 ± 116 N·m; women 245; passive tissues 25 N·m arched to 120 N·m fully flexed); Cholewicki J, McGill SM, Norman RW (1991). Lumbar spine loads during the lifting of extremely heavy weights. Med Sci Sports Exerc 23(10):1179–1186. doi:10.1249/00005768-199110000-00012 (national powerlifting championship deadlifts: L4/L5 moments up to 988 N·m on average for the heaviest lifts)

grip.note: Men's median peak grip (ages 29–39, best of both hands, crush grip on a dynamometer). Holding a bar isn't a crush grip (the hand wraps a fixed handle), so this is a rough capacity.
grip.source: Dodds RM, Syddall HE, Cooper R, Benzeval M, Deary IJ, Dennison EM, et al. (2014). Grip strength across the life course: normative data from twelve British studies. PLoS ONE 9(12):e113637. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0113637 (49,964 participants; women's peak median 31 kg)

holdingStrengthNote: Rough capacities for the holding (isometric) loads, so they can show an effort: men's values, scaled by the strength slider (an entry {nm} for a torque, {kgPerHand} for the grip). The upper back, neck and shoulder blades have no usable norm yet (Garcés et al. 2002's neck values are given in N in the text but labelled N·m in the tables).
massNote: mass: fraction of body mass per segment (one leg or arm; the masses sum to 1 for the whole body). com: centre of mass as a fraction of segment length, measured from the ankle (shank), knee (thigh), hip (head + trunk), shoulder (upper arm) or elbow (forearm + hand, along elbow → grip). From de Leva's table for young adult males; head + trunk is the mass-weighted combination (head centre of mass placed about 0.13 m above the trunk's top), which lands at 66% of hip → shoulder.
source: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
